name: Good AI Practice in Manufacturing
blurb: The FDA and EMA principles applied to production.
title: Good AI Practice in Manufacturing
answer: The ten FDA and EMA principles of good AI practice explicitly include manufacturing. For plants this means risk based use, high quality data, documented models, and monitoring through the product lifecycle.

reading.body:
The FDA and EMA's ten principles of good AI practice cover manufacturing, and they add no new binding rules, only the expectation that existing GMP applies to AI.

That distinction is the practical content here. A plant adopting AI does not face a separate regulatory regime. It faces the same regime read through AI: risk based use, high quality data, documented models, and monitoring across the product lifecycle. The principles are guidance on how existing requirements land on these systems, not a new layer above them.

The recommended home for them is the site quality manual and its procedures, so that every AI project inherits the same expectations by default. That matters because the alternative is per project governance, rebuilt each time and hard for an inspector to recognise. Writing the principles into the manual also settles the question of where accountability sits, which is the plant, not the vendor or the model.

What this does not cover is the substance of validation, data integrity, or specific applications such as inspection, predictive maintenance, or digital twins. Those are separate subjects. Nor does the data say how the principles are enforced, what an inspector will ask for, or how the FDA and EMA differ in emphasis. It establishes that manufacturing is in scope and where the rules should live, and stops there.

explainer:
The FDA and EMA principles apply to manufacturing as much as to clinical work. In a plant they translate into concrete practices: decide where AI is justified by assessing risk, use representative and well governed data, document how models were built and tested, assess performance in the actual operating context, monitor through the lifecycle, and give operators clear information about what a system does and its limits.

Building these into the site quality manual and standard procedures means every new AI project inherits them by default rather than reinventing governance each time, and it gives inspectors a recognisable structure.
